A_target.statement:
In a two-player [[Definition:Zero-Sum Game|zero-sum game]] with payoff $u$ to player $A$, the minimizing player $B$'s optimal value satisfies:
:$\displaystyle \min_{\text {moves} } u = -\max_{\text {moves} } \paren {-u}$
so the game tree is evaluated by the single [[Definition:Negamax|negamax]] recursion.

B_source.statement:
The optimal value at a node where one player moves is:
:$\displaystyle \map V n = \max_{c \mathop \in \map {\operatorname {children} } n} \map V c$

derived.the recursion alternating between player: a single recursion using negation at each level
derived.two separate cases in the search: one uniform case, since negation absorbs the alternation

object_map.reformulation: Absorb the alternation between players into a negation, so that both levels become maximization.

validity_conditions: The game is zero sum, so one player's payoff is exactly the negation of the other's, which is what licenses replacing minimization by negated maximization.
Negation is an order-reversing involution, so applying it twice returns the original value and the alternation is consistent at every depth.
The reformulation changes only the presentation, not the computed value, so any search optimization valid for one form remains valid for the other.
proof_plan: The game is zero-sum, so the payoff to $B$ is $-u$.

Replace minimization over moves by negated maximization:
:$\displaystyle \min_c \map V c = -\max_c \paren {-\map V c}$
As negation is an [[Definition:Involution (Mapping)|involution]], alternating levels compose correctly.

Collapse the two cases into the single recursion:
:$\displaystyle \map {V'} n = \max_{c \mathop \in \map {\operatorname {children} } n} \paren {-\map {V'} c}$
with $\map {V'} n$ the value to the player to move at $n$.
{{qed}}
